message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"4.6","text":"And I said, “If our lord Peter did not know that he alone can prevail over that man’s power, he would not have sent us ahead with instructions to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon and to write it to him.” All the same, since evening had overtaken us, we partook of salt and slept. In the morning, someone acquainted with Bernice came and said that Simon had sailed away to Sidon but had left behind some of his disciples: Appion the many-times victor, an Alexandrian man and a grammarian by training, whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father; Annubion the Diospolitan, a certain astrologer; and Athenodorus the Athenian, who approved of the teaching of Epicurus. After learning what concerned Simon, we wrote everything down at dawn and sent it on to Peter, and then went off for a walk.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Πέτρος","chosen":"our lord Peter","rationale":"The human honorific κύριος is retained as “lord” rather than recast as a theological title."},{"source_quote":"λανθανόντως τὰ κατὰ Σίμωνα διαμανθάνοντας","chosen":"to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon","rationale":"διαμανθάνω conveys thorough learning, while λανθανόντως indicates that it was to be done secretly or unnoticed."},{"source_quote":"ἁλῶν μεταλαβόντες","chosen":"we partook of salt","rationale":"The wording literally invokes sharing salt and can idiomatically denote taking food; the concrete image is preserved."},{"source_quote":"Ἀππίωνα τὸν πλειστονίκην","chosen":"Appion the many-times victor","rationale":"πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet meaning one who has won very many victories; it could alternatively be presented as the title or name “Pleistonikes.”"},{"source_quote":"ὃν πρὸς πατρός μοι φίλον ὄντα ἐπέγνων","chosen":"whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father","rationale":"πρὸς πατρός indicates a paternal connection. Possible nuances include “a paternal family friend” or “my father’s friend.”"},{"source_quote":"τῷ Ἐπικούρου ἀρεσκόμενον λόγῳ","chosen":"who approved of the teaching of Epicurus","rationale":"ἀρεσκόμενον expresses being pleased with or approving Epicurus’s λόγος; “approved of” avoids implying the stronger allegiance suggested by “devoted.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς","issue":"The printed accentuation gives ὁμῶς, ordinarily associated with “alike,” while the context supports the concessive force of ὅμως, “nevertheless” or “all the same.” The supplied form can still be represented contextually as “All the same.”","proposed_reading":"ὅμως","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.7","text":"And Appion met us, not only with the two companions already mentioned but also with about thirty other men. As soon as he saw me, he greeted me, kissed me warmly, and said, “This is Clement, about whose noble birth and freeborn dignity I have spoken to you at length, telling you that, although he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar and has been trained in every branch of Greek education, he has been deceived by a certain barbarian named Peter into doing and saying the things of the Jews. I therefore ask you to join me in the effort to correct him. And in your presence I question the man himself. Let him tell me this: since he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious, how is he not committing the gravest impieties by abandoning his ancestral customs and turning aside to barbarian ways?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπηντᾶτο ἡμῖν","chosen":"met us","rationale":"The imperfect can describe Appion encountering or coming to meet the group."},{"source_quote":"τῆς τε εὐγενείας καὶ τῆς ἐλευθεροπρεπείας","chosen":"his noble birth and freeborn dignity","rationale":"εὐγένεια concerns distinguished birth, while ἐλευθεροπρέπεια denotes dignity or conduct befitting a free person; “generosity” or “magnificence” is also possible for the latter."},{"source_quote":"πολὺν ἐποιούμην λόγον, ὅτι","chosen":"I have spoken to you at length, telling you that","rationale":"ὅτι is taken as introducing the content of Appion’s prior account and is therefore explicitly connected to λόγον. It could alternatively be causal—“I spoke at length because …”—but the reporting attachment provides a natural transition into what Appion had said about Clement."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς γένους Τιβερίου Καίσαρος ὢν","chosen":"he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar","rationale":"The phrase presents Clement as related to or descended from Tiberius Caesar’s family."},{"source_quote":"τὰ Ἰουδαίων ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν","chosen":"doing and saying the things of the Jews","rationale":"The elliptical τὰ Ἰουδαίων is preserved broadly rather than narrowed to particular Jewish rites or doctrines."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ἐφ’ ὑμῶν αὐτοῦ πυνθάνομαι","chosen":"And in your presence I question the man himself","rationale":"ἐφ’ ὑμῶν means “before/in the presence of you,” and the genitive αὐτοῦ is naturally taken with πυνθάνομαι as the person questioned."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸ εὐσεβεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἀποδεδωκέναι","chosen":"he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious","rationale":"ἀποδίδωμι with the reflexive expresses giving or devoting oneself to an undertaking."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἑτέρων’ ἀνδρῶν","issue":"The raised apostrophe after ἑτέρων is syntactically inert and appears to be anomalous editorial punctuation. It does not affect the sentence’s meaning.","proposed_reading":"ἑτέρων ἀνδρῶν","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάτρια,’ ἀποκλίνας","issue":"The apostrophe beside the comma after πάτρια appears to be an extraneous editorial mark. The participial construction remains clear.","proposed_reading":"τὰ πάτρια, ἀποκλίνας","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"4.8","text":"And I answered, “I welcome your good intention toward me, but I reject your ignorance. The intention is good, because you want me to be among those things you regard as good; but your understanding, being unsound, strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me.” Appion said, “Does it seem to you to be ignorance for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks?” And I answered, “One who chooses to be pious need not invariably observe ancestral customs. He should observe them if they are pious, but cast them off if they prove impious. For someone born of an impious father may wish to be pious and therefore not wish to follow the object of his father’s worship.” Appion replied, “What then? Are you saying that your father lived a wicked life?” And I said, “His life was not wicked, but his belief was.” Appion said, “What was this wicked notion of his? I want to hear.” And I said, “He believed the false and wicked myths of the Greeks.” Appion asked, “Which are these myths of the Greeks that are both false and wicked?” And I said, “The wrong conception of gods, which, if you are patient, you will hear about together with those who are eager to learn.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν δὲ ἀγνωσίαν ἀποσείομαι","chosen":"but I reject your ignorance","rationale":"ἀποσείω literally suggests shaking something off and here expresses firm rejection."},{"source_quote":"ἡ δὲ γνῶσις οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἔχουσα","chosen":"but your understanding, being unsound","rationale":"γνῶσις contrasts with ἀγνωσία and denotes Appion’s understanding or judgment, which Clement considers incorrectly disposed."},{"source_quote":"φιλίας προφάσει ἐνεδρεύειν ἀγωνίζεται","chosen":"strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me","rationale":"The martial image of lying in ambush is retained; “for me” supplies the contextually evident target."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάτρια ἔθη φυλάττοντα τὰ Ἑλλήνων φρονεῖν","chosen":"for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks","rationale":"τὰ Ἑλλήνων is elliptical, literally “the things of the Greeks,” and in this argumentative context denotes Greek beliefs or opinions."},{"source_quote":"τῷ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀκολουθεῖν σεβάσματι","chosen":"to follow the object of his father’s worship","rationale":"σέβασμα can denote an object of reverence or worship; “his father’s religion” is a broader possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"Κακοῦ μὲν οὐκ ἦν βίου, κακῆς δὲ ὑπολήψεως","chosen":"His life was not wicked, but his belief was","rationale":"The compact nominal contrast between βίος and ὑπόληψις is expressed idiomatically while preserving the repeated evaluation as wicked."},{"source_quote":"Ἡ περὶ θεῶν οὐκ ὀρθὴ δόκησις","chosen":"The wrong conception of gods","rationale":"δόκησις denotes an opinion or conception; the phrase does not itself specify one particular doctrine about the gods."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.9","text":"“Therefore, before the discussions, let us now withdraw to some quieter place; there I will converse with you. This is the reason I have wished to speak in private: neither the many nor even all those who practice philosophy approach the judgment of things that exist sincerely. For we know many, even among those who take great pride in philosophy, who seek empty glory or have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money rather than for virtue itself. If they do not find what they practice philosophy for, they turn to scoffing. Because of such people, then, let us choose a place suitable for being by ourselves.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τοῦ δὲ ἰδιολογεῖσθαί με βούλεσθαι","chosen":"I have wished to speak in private","rationale":"ἰδιολογέομαι denotes holding a private or separate conversation."},{"source_quote":"τῇ τῶν ὄντων κρίσει","chosen":"the judgment of things that exist","rationale":"The philosophical expression may also be rendered “the examination of realities”; the more source-transparent wording preserves τὰ ὄντα."},{"source_quote":"κενοδοξοῦντας","chosen":"who seek empty glory","rationale":"The compound describes vainglorious conduct or pursuit of baseless prestige."},{"source_quote":"χρηματισμοῦ χάριν περιβεβλημένους τὸν τρίβωνα","chosen":"have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money","rationale":"The τρίβων is the worn cloak conventionally associated with philosophers; the image is retained rather than replaced with a general reference to pretending to be philosophers."},{"source_quote":"ἐὰν μὴ εὕρωσιν δι’ ὃ φιλοσοφοῦσιν","chosen":"If they do not find what they practice philosophy for","rationale":"The wording leaves the desired objective implicit; it may refer to empty prestige, financial gain, or either motive just mentioned."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸ ἰδιάζειν","chosen":"suitable for being by ourselves","rationale":"ἰδιάζω here means withdrawing from the public or remaining in private, in parallel with the preceding wish for private conversation."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"4.10","text":"And a certain wealthy man among them, who also always possessed around himself a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves, said, “Since the heat is blazing fiercely, let us withdraw a short distance from the city, into my gardens.” And so, after going on, they seated themselves where there were clear streams of cool spring water and a green canopy of trees of every kind. There I gladly sat down, with the rest around me. As they remained silent, in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me, they showed by staring at me that they were demanding the fulfillment of the promise. And so I began to speak in this way.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σφόδρα καῦμα ἐπιφλέγει","chosen":"the heat is blazing fiercely","rationale":"ἐπιφλέγω presents the heat as burning or blazing upon them, and σφόδρα supplies the intensity."},{"source_quote":"βραχὺ τῆς πόλεως","chosen":"a short distance from the city","rationale":"The accusative βραχύ expresses a small extent of distance."},{"source_quote":"καθαρὰ ψυχρῶν ναμάτων ῥεύματα","chosen":"clear streams of cool spring water","rationale":"νάματα denotes flowing or spring water, while ῥεύματα emphasizes its streams or currents."},{"source_quote":"δένδρων παντοίων χλοερὰ σκέπη","chosen":"a green canopy of trees of every kind","rationale":"σκέπη is shelter or covering; in the garden setting, “canopy” conveys the trees’ green overhead cover."},{"source_quote":"ἀντὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀξιοῦν με φωνῆς","chosen":"in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me","rationale":"The voice is personified as about to appeal to Clement. The wording is elliptical about the requested action, which the following clause identifies as fulfillment of the promise."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ὑποσχέσεως τὴν ἀπόδειξιν","chosen":"the fulfillment of the promise","rationale":"ἀπόδειξις literally denotes demonstration or proof; here it is the promised exposition whose delivery the listeners demand."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"καὶ διὰ παντὸς χῶρόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτὸν κεκτημένος παμμούσων φύλλων","issue":"The image-checked supplied reading literally describes the man as continually possessing around himself “a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves.” The application of παμμούσων, denoting accomplishment in all the arts, to φύλλων, “leaves,” is contextually anomalous and may reflect corruption, but that possibility is not established. The main text therefore preserves a defensible literal representation of the selected edition. A possible conjecture is χορόν, “company,” for χῶρόν and φίλων, “friends,” for φύλλων, yielding a company of friends accomplished in every art; this conjecture has not been substituted into the translation.","proposed_reading":"καὶ διὰ παντὸς χορόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτὸν κεκτημένος παμμούσων φίλων","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
